title: Chapter 50: The Roof Garden, Part 3 of 5: Up the Hill
html:
The Hill began where the shops stopped having prices in the window.
Corin had never thought of it like that before. But it was true. At the bottom of Exchange Street the windows had cards in them, written in big letters, GLOVES 2s. 6d. BEST QUALITY, HATS RE-TRIMMED, TEA, FINE, BY THE OUNCE. Halfway up, the cards got smaller and the writing got prettier. And then, at the top of Exchange Street, where the road turned and began to climb in earnest, the cards stopped altogether. The windows had one thing in them each, a single hat on a stand, a single pair of gloves laid on a velvet cushion, a single blue bottle of scent with a gold stopper, and no price at all. As if anyone who needed to ask was on the wrong street.
The road climbed.
It was steep, here, and the brown mare felt it. She put her head down and leaned into the collar and went slowly, one big feathered foot after another, and the cart groaned behind her. Abner did not hurry her. He sat on his seat with the reins loose in his black hands, and every so often he said something to her, very low, that Corin could not hear. The mare's ears went back to listen each time, and then forward again.
The snow was cleaner up here. Somebody swept it. All along both sides of the road there were boys with brooms, in the doorways and at the corners, sweeping the steps of the great houses and the crossings of the streets, and the snow they swept was piled in neat white heaps along the gutters, like sugar. The houses were taller, and whiter, and further apart. They had iron railings in front of them, with gilt tips like spears. They had steps going up to their front doors, and lamps on brackets by the doors, and knockers shaped like lions' heads and dolphins and hands.
They passed the end of Velvet Street.
Corin did not mean to look down it. He looked anyway.
It was a short street, and narrow for the Hill, with small fine shops on both sides, close together. A milliner's. A glover's. A shop that sold nothing but fans. And halfway down on the left, a shop with a big bow window of small square panes, and gold letters on the glass that he could just read from the corner.
THE NEEDLE AND THIMBLE.
The shutters were up. Every one. There was a black bow of crape tied on the door handle, big and limp and wet with snow. And on the door itself, nailed up, there was a white paper that Corin could not read from here but did not need to. By order of the Watch. There would be a word on it that he knew. The Watch had only one word for what had happened in that shop on Thursday afternoon.
On the step in front of the shut door, somebody had put a little bunch of flowers. Winter flowers, white and green, from a hothouse somewhere. They were lying in the snow, already going brown at the edges.
Corin looked at them until the cart had gone past the end of the street. He thought about four pins in an old woman's mouth. About a red cushion on a wrist. Madame Hesper. Agnes. She held her door.
Juno, beside him, had seen it too. She did not say anything. She put her hand on his arm, on the leather cape, for a moment, and then took it away.
They came out onto the Crescent.
Corin had heard about the Crescent. He had never been on it. Lyra had told him about it, on Saturday night, a week ago, coming back from the Duke's with her mother's memory gone out of her. It's white. All of it. White houses in a curve, all the way round the top of the Hill, like a smile. And the gas lamps. The city pays for the gas. She had said it in a flat voice, the way she said things she did not want to feel.
It was white. It was very white. A long smooth curve of tall white houses, all joined together, all exactly the same height, with tall windows and black railings and white steps, going round and round the top of the Hill as far as Corin could see. In front of the houses ran a wide road, swept clean, and in front of the road there was a garden, long and narrow, following the curve, with bare trees in it and white paths and a little frozen fountain. And all along the road, on both sides, there were tall iron lamp-posts, painted green, with glass lamps on top. Gas. Even now, at the first bell after noon, on a gray winter day, the lamps were lit. Every one. They burned with a soft steady white-blue flame behind their glass, all the way round the Crescent, so that the whole long white curve of it seemed to glow.
The city paid for the gas. The river parishes paid for the city.
Abner turned the mare left, along the Crescent. Slowly.
They passed a house with a door covered all over in gold leaf, so that it shone like a coin, and two footmen on the steps in gold coats. Marrow House. Corin knew it from Lyra's telling. There was a carriage at the door, a dark blue one, and a coachman on the box, and two gray horses. Not Tibbs's grays. Some other pair. The Duke's Saturdays began at the second bell. People were coming early.
They passed the end of a street going off to the right, a short wide street lined with tall houses, with a big house at the end of it with all its shutters closed and a stone girl with a jug standing in the garden in front. Crown Walk. That house is the Duke's now, Lyra had told him last night, in the vault, very quietly. He bought it. He keeps it shut. He has the only key. My mother asked him to.
Corin looked at the shut house for as long as he could.
And then, from behind them, he heard horses.
Not a cart horse. Carriage horses. Two of them, by the sound, trotting, light and quick, on the swept road. And wheels, not iron-rimmed like Abner's but rubber or leather, whispering on the stones. And a voice, a young man's voice, calling out cheerfully, Way, there! Way, coal!
Abner pulled the mare over to the side of the road, against the garden railings, without looking round. Coal carts always pulled over. Coal carts were always in the way.
The carriage came up beside them.
It was a neat small carriage, a closed one, very clean, painted dark green, with yellow wheels. Two bay horses, glossy, with their breath going up in clouds. A coachman on the box in a green coat and a hat with a cockade, a young man with a round pink cheerful face and a long nose, who was whistling. A nice lad. Bit simple. And on the door of the carriage, painted on a round blue enamel badge the size of a dinner plate, a white hand holding up a small gold lamp.
The carriage slowed a little, to pass them on the narrow road.
And for a moment, perhaps three breaths, perhaps four, it was right beside them. Its window was level with Corin's face, an arm's length away, on the other side of a row of coal sacks.
The window was down. Just a little. A hand's width.
There was a smell. It came out of the window in a warm puff, the way warm air comes out of a door in winter. Corin knew it before he knew that he knew it. Peppermint. Sweet and sharp and cold. And under the peppermint, very faint, so faint that most people would never have smelled it at all, something else. Something dry and green and bitter, like old hay. Like a graveyard in summer.
Grayroot.
Inside the carriage, on the seat, a man was sitting with his hands folded on top of an ebony stick.
He was thin and narrow-shouldered and not very tall, in a gray coat with a gray fur collar. He had gray gloves on. His hair was white and fine, like thistledown, and stood up a little round his pink scalp, and he had a round pink face, very clean, very kind, like a baby's face that had grown old without noticing. He wore small gold spectacles. And on the seat beside him, on the green leather, there was a little round box of silver, very polished, the size of a pocket watch.
He was smiling.
He was not smiling at anything. He was just smiling, to himself, looking out of the window at the Crescent going by. At the white houses and the gas lamps and the garden. The way a man smiles who has had a good lunch and is going somewhere pleasant.
His eyes went over the coal cart.
They went over the sacks, and the brown mare, and Abner's broad black back on the seat. And over Juno, small and muffled in her three shawls. And over Corin. Over a black face under a leather cap, a coal man's lad with a leg in splints, sitting on a sack. They did not stop. They did not change. They went over him the way eyes go over a lamp-post, or a heap of swept snow. And then they went on, to the garden, and the fountain, and the bare trees.
On Friday, at the Fish Stairs, those same eyes had looked down at Corin lying gray on a dead-barrow under a card that said FEVER, and Pallister had said, softly, kindly, How very gray he is. And he had leaned down and put a sweet on Corin's chest.
Today he did not see him at all.
The carriage went by. The young coachman touched his hat to Abner, cheerfully, as one man on a box to another. Thank you, coal! And then the bay horses were trotting on along the Crescent, quick and light, and the yellow wheels were whispering on the swept road, and the green carriage was going away from them round the long white curve, toward the top of the Hill.
Corin let out his breath. He had not known he was holding it.
Juno was looking at him.
"That was him," she said. It was not a question.
"That was him."
"He looked right at you."
"He looked at coal," said Corin.
Abner Cole, on the seat, said nothing at all. He just clicked his tongue at the brown mare, very softly, and pulled her out from the railings again, and they went on along the Crescent after the green carriage. Slowly. A coal cart behind a gentleman's carriage, going the same way, which was the way all the carriages went on a Saturday afternoon on the Hill.
Up.
At the far end of the Crescent, where the long white curve of houses ended, the road went on climbing. It went up between two tall stone pillars with stone urns on top of them, and through a gap in a high wall, and up a short steep slope with trees on both sides, old dark trees, cedars, with snow lying on their flat black branches like cloth on a table.
And at the top of the slope, against the gray sky, filling it, there was the palace.
Corin had seen it all his life. Everyone in the city had seen it all their lives. You could see it from anywhere. From the river, from the Saltmarsh, from the roof of the Ministry. A great round white dome on top of the Hill, above everything, sitting on its ring of white walls like an egg in a cup. You saw it every day, and you stopped seeing it, the way you stopped seeing the sky.
He had never been this close.
It was enormous. That was the first thing. It was so much bigger than it looked from below. The walls went up and up, white stone, smooth, with rows of tall windows in them, and every window had a little stone balcony, and every balcony had a stone urn. Above the walls there was a ring of columns, white, standing all the way round. And above the columns, the dome. White. Not snow-white. It was made of something that was already white under the snow. Some kind of stone, or glass, or both, that shone very faintly even on a day like this, the way a pearl shines. And out of the very top of the dome there rose the spire. Tall and white and so thin that it went up into the low gray clouds and was lost in them, like a needle going into cloth. At the top of it, the Ledger said, there was a great stone eye, open, the same as the eye carved over the doors of the Ministry, looking out over the whole city. Corin could not see it today. The clouds had it. But he felt it, the way he had felt it in the autumn, from the street of white houses below. In the river parishes the old people still called this place the temple, not the palace. Corin had never known why.
The green carriage was going up to the front of it. Up a wide straight drive, between two rows of clipped dark yew trees, toward a pair of great gates in the white wall. The gates were tall and black and gilded, and on each side of them there was a guard. Two guards. In white. White coats and white trousers and tall white hats, and silver at their shoulders. They stood so still that Corin had thought at first that they were statues.
The gates opened for the green carriage without anybody seeming to open them. It went through. They closed.
Abner Cole did not go up the drive.
He turned the brown mare to the right, very slowly, off the road, onto a narrow lane that ran along the outside of the white wall, under the dark cedars, going round. A lane with deep ruts in the snow, and no boys with brooms. A back way.
"Coal goes round the back," he said, to nobody, without turning round. "Always has."
The Back Gate
The lane went round the palace the long way, the way back lanes always do.
It ran along the foot of the white wall under the cedars, and the wall went up beside them, smooth and blank and very high, three times the height of a man, with no windows in it at all down here. The lane was in shadow. The cedars kept the light off, and kept the snow off too, mostly, so that under their branches there was only a thin gray crust of old snow on the ruts, and dead brown needles, and the smell of resin. It was very quiet. Corin could hear the brown mare's breathing, and the creak of the cart, and the drip of snow melting off the cedar branches somewhere, slow, tap, tap, like a clock.
Then the lane began to go down.
The top of the Hill was not flat. Corin had always thought it was, from below. But the palace had been built right on the edge of it, on the eastern side, where the Hill fell away steeply toward the river. So that from the front, from the drive and the gates, it looked as if it stood on level ground. And from the back, the ground dropped away under it, and the white walls went down and down with the slope, and the palace was taller at the back than at the front. Much taller. A whole wing of it, on the east side, stood out from the main walls on great stone arches, like a bridge that went nowhere, with rooms on top. And the top of that wing was flat. Corin could see the edge of it from the lane, high above, a long line of white stone against the gray sky, with something growing along it. The bare twigs of trees, very small. Bushes. And the top of a little glass roof, catching the light.
A garden. On a roof.
He looked at it until the cedars closed in again and hid it.
The lane went down past the arches. Under one of them, through a great curved tunnel of white stone, dripping and cold, and out the other side. And on the other side, set into the foot of the white wall, there was the back gate.
It was not a gate like the front gates. It was a plain arch, in the wall, as wide as a cart, with a pair of heavy wooden doors in it studded with iron nails and bound with iron straps. The doors were shut. To one side of them there was a little gatehouse, built into the wall, with a small window and a smaller door, and a thin line of smoke going up from a chimney. And to the other side, set into the foot of the wall at the level of the lane, there was a square iron flap, black and rusty, with a ring on it. The coal chute.
And above the arch, on a long iron hook, there hung a lamp.
Corin saw it as soon as they came out from under the tunnel. He felt it before he saw it. A prickle in his fingers, in the gray, under the coal dust. A prickle like the feeling just before frost-bite, when your fingers start to burn instead of freeze. He looked up.
It was brass. A tall brass lamp with a round glass belly, like the one he had seen at the kitchen door of the Bourse, and the one by the wet door. The one that had burned his hands on Sunday night until they smoked. It was not lit. Not with a flame. But inside the round glass there was something, a faint soft glow, pale and greenish, like the light in a marsh at night. It moved a little. It turned in the glass the way a fish turns in a bowl, slowly, as if it were looking for something.
An Ash lamp.
They found Ash. That was what they were for. They found harvesters, and the burned-out places that harvesters carried in them, and the gray. Gant had them. The Bourse had them, on the doors that mattered. And the Archon's palace had one here, over the back gate, where the coal came in.
Corin put his hands under the leather cape.
It did not help much. The prickle got worse as the cart rolled nearer. It went up from his fingers into his wrists, into his arms. Into the place behind his left ear, the patch of gray there that the lamp at the wet door had burned on Sunday. That patch began to sting. He set his teeth.
Juno looked at him.
"What is it?"
"The lamp."
She looked up at it. She went white under her shawls.
Abner Cole stopped the cart beside the coal chute. He stopped it a little further on than the chute, Corin noticed. Further from the arch than he needed to. So that the cart was ten yards from the hanging lamp instead of five. He did it without looking round. Then he climbed down off his seat, slow and heavy, and went to the little gatehouse door, and knocked on it with one black knuckle.
The door opened.
An old man looked out. He was small and stooped and neat, with a gray coat buttoned to the chin and a white band round his arm with a stone eye stitched on it in gray. He had a pen behind his ear, and gray whiskers, and the face of a man who had been sitting by a small fire for a very long time and did not want to get up.
"Cole," he said.
"Mister Prowse."
"Forty?"
"Forty."
The old man nodded. He went back inside. Through the little window Corin could see him at a high sloping desk, like a clerk's desk, with a big book open on it. He dipped the pen. He wrote. Then he looked up, through the window, at the cart.
He came back to the door.
"Who's that?" he said.
Abner did not look round.
"My lad," he said. "And the girl's my sister's. Helping."
"You never have a lad."
"I've got one now." Abner spat into the snow, the way he had spat at the barrier. "Leg's broke. Coal sack. Tuesday. Won't stay home. I told him. He won't."
Mister Prowse looked at the cart for a long moment.
Above the arch, the brass lamp turned in its hook. Very slowly. The pale green glow inside its glass belly moved, and leaned, the way a candle flame leans in a draft. Leaned toward the cart. Toward Corin.
Corin could not breathe. The stinging behind his ear was like a burn now, a real one, as if someone were holding a hot coin there. His hands under the cape had started to ache, a deep ache, in the bones.
Mister Prowse looked up at the lamp.
He frowned.
"Restless today," he said.
Abner Cole looked up at it too. Slowly. He looked at it for a while, with his white eyes in his black face. Then he shrugged his big shoulders.
"It's the coal," he said. "Always is. It's dug out of the dead, coal is. Old trees. Old things. Down in the dark. My father used to say that lamp never liked his coal neither." He rubbed his nose with his black knuckle. "Never liked him much, come to that."
The old man looked at him.
Then, unexpectedly, he laughed. A short dry wheezing laugh, like a door that needs oiling.
"No," he said. "No, it never did. I remember." He shook his head. He went back inside, to his book, and dipped his pen again, and wrote something more. And Corin, staring at him through the little window with the lamp burning behind his ear, saw his lips move as he wrote it.
Cole. Coal. Forty. And two lads.
He put the pen back behind his ear and shut his door. The smoke went on going up from his chimney.
Abner Cole went to the iron flap in the wall, and took hold of the ring, and pulled it up. It came up with a long rusty scream. Under it there was a square black hole, going down into the dark, and a breath of warm air came up out of it, warm and dusty and smelling of the inside of a great house. Of fires, and baking bread, and hot water, and polish.
Then he came back to the cart, and pulled the first sack to the edge, and turned round, and bent his knees, and swung it up onto his back over the leather cape. It must have weighed as much as a man. He carried it the four steps to the chute, and bent, and tipped it, and the coal went down into the dark with a long roaring rattle, like a drum roll.
He came back for the second.
Juno was already sliding down off the cart. She landed on the sides of her feet in their huge boots and staggered and caught herself on the wheel.
"Get back up," said Corin.
"No."
"Juno—"
"There's forty. He can't do forty on his own. Not fast. Not if we want to be gone before the fourth bell." She reached up and took hold of the corner of the next sack and pulled it toward her, to the edge, the way she had seen Abner do it. She could not lift it. She did not try to lift it. She just pulled it to the edge of the cart and held it there, so that Abner, coming back, could turn and bend and take it straight onto his back without having to reach. And then she turned to the next one.
Abner looked at her. He did not tell her to stop.
Corin sat on his sack with his hands under his cape and the lamp burning behind his ear and watched them, and knew he could not sit here for an hour. He could not sit here for a quarter of an hour. The ache in his hands was getting worse. The lamp was still leaning. And there were thirty-eight sacks to go.
He looked up the lane.
On the far side of the back gate, past the gatehouse and the chute, the lane went on round the foot of the palace. And just beyond the chute, set into the white wall, there was an opening. A narrow gap between the palace wall and the wall of the next house along, the wall of somebody's great garden. And in the gap, going up, there were steps.
Stone steps. Narrow and steep and very old, worn hollow in the middle, with an iron handrail on one side, fixed into the palace wall, rusty and cold. They went up and up between the two high walls, in a crack of gray daylight, and turned a corner at the top, and were gone.
There was a little iron sign at the bottom of them, on the wall, with words on it in raised letters that somebody had once painted white.
GARDEN STEPS. PUBLIC WAY.
Corin looked at them.
Then he looked at Abner, coming back for the fourth sack.
"Where do they go?" he said.
Abner stopped. He looked at the steps. He looked at Corin's leg.
"Up," he said. "To Spire Row. Behind the palace, at the top. It's the old way, from before they built the drive. Nobody uses it now. It's steep. And it's cold." He bent and took the sack onto his back. "There's a bit, at the top, by the first turn, where you can see over."
"Over what?"
Abner Cole carried the sack to the chute and tipped it. The coal roared down into the dark. Then he straightened, slowly, and looked back at Corin, over the black sack on his shoulder.
"Over the wall," he said. "Into the garden. Her garden." He looked away again. "My father used to take his pipe up there. On a Saturday. While the boy did the sacks. Said it was the only garden on the Hill a coal man could look at for nothing."
And behind Corin's ear, the lamp burned, and burned.
The Garden Steps
Getting down off the cart was the first hard thing.
He did it on his own. Abner was carrying, and Juno was pulling sacks, and he did not want either of them to stop. So he put the crutch down first, over the side, into the snow, and got his good leg under him, and swung the bad one over the edge of the boards with both hands, like a man lifting a log over a wall. And then he slid. Down off the edge of the cart, onto the good foot, with the crutch under his arm, and the bad leg sticking out in front of him in its splints like a plank.
He did not fall. He nearly did. He stood in the snow for a moment by the wheel, swaying, with his teeth shut so hard that his jaw hurt, and the lamp over the arch burning behind his ear, and waited for the world to stop going round.
It stopped.
"Where are you going?" said Juno sharply, from the cart.
"Up there."
She looked at the steps. She looked at him.
"You can't."
"I can go up stairs sideways," said Corin. "Silas said so. It's one of the things I can still do."
"Silas didn't mean those."
"He didn't say which ones."
Juno opened her mouth. Then she shut it again, and looked at the lamp over the arch, and at his face under the coal dust, and he saw her understand. She did not argue. She was fourteen, and she had grown up on roofs, and she knew what it was like when there was only one way off a place and you had to take it.
"I'll come when we're done," she said. "Forty sacks. Don't go any further than the turn."
"I won't."
"And don't fall off."
"I'll try not to."
He went along the foot of the wall, past the gatehouse, past the open chute with its warm breath coming up out of the dark, swinging the bad leg from the hip the way Silas had shown him. Crutch, good foot. Crutch, good foot. The bad leg swung along between them, stiff, its heel dragging a line in the snow. He kept his head down. He kept his black hands in the cape as much as he could. He did not look at the gatehouse window. He felt Mister Prowse look at him through it, and then look away again, back to his book and his fire.
And with every step he took away from the arch, the burning behind his ear got a little less.
By the time he reached the bottom of the steps it was only a sting. By the time he had his hand on the cold iron rail, it was only an ache. The lamp was behind him, round the curve of the wall. He let out a long breath, and leaned on the rail, and looked up.
The steps went up between the two walls like water going up a gully.
They were very narrow. Not much wider than his shoulders. On the right, the palace wall, smooth and white and enormous, with the iron rail fixed into it at the height of his hip by iron pins every few feet. On the left, the other wall, older and rougher, gray stone gone green with damp, with ivy growing over the top of it, black and dead with the winter. Between the two walls there was a strip of gray sky, high up, very narrow, like the gap between two pages of a book. The light came down into the gap thin and cold. Snow had blown into it and lay on the steps in little drifts, on the outside edge of each one, away from the rail. The middle of each step was worn hollow, like the inside of a spoon, from a hundred years of feet.
He began to climb.
He did it the way Silas had told him to on Wednesday, sitting on the bench in the crypt, with the leg out in front of him. Sideways. Good leg first. Always. Good leg goes up, bad leg follows. Bad leg goes down first, good leg follows. Up with the good, down with the bad. Say it. And Corin had said it, feeling like a child learning a rhyme. Up with the good. Down with the bad.
So he turned sideways on the steps, with his right side to the palace wall and his right hand on the rail, and the crutch in his left hand, on the step below him. And he put his good foot, the right, up on the first step. And pulled. With his hand on the rail, and his good leg, and his whole back. And the bad leg came up after, swinging, stiff, and the heel of it knocked on the edge of the step and the pain went up through the thigh like a nail. And then the crutch came up. And he was on the first step.
He stood there and breathed.
Then he did it again.
He counted them. He could not help it. He had been counting steps all autumn. Lyra counted everything, and he had caught it from her like a cold. One. Two. Three. Each one was the same. Good foot up. Pull. Bad leg, knock, nail. Crutch. Breathe. Seven. Eight. The cold iron of the rail burned his black palm through the coal dust. The gray in his fingers did not feel the cold, but the place where the gray ended, at the wrist, felt it, and ached. Twelve. His good thigh began to shake. Fifteen. Sweat came out on his face under the coal dust, and ran, and he thought of Vespera's paint, running with sweat, and was glad it was coal and not paint. Coal did not mind sweat. Coal just got blacker.
Twenty.
He stopped. He leaned on the rail with his forehead against the cold white stone of the palace wall and shut his eyes.
The palace was very quiet on the other side of the wall. He could not hear anything at all through it. Not a voice. Not a footstep. Not a door. It was like leaning his head against a cliff.
Twenty-one.
He went on.
At the thirtieth step the snow was deeper, and his crutch slipped, and for a moment he hung on the rail with one hand and his whole weight on it and his good foot scrabbling on the worn stone, and the bad leg dragging, and he thought, very clearly, This is how it ends. Not in a fire. Not on a glass floor. On a public stair, at the back of a palace, in a coal man's cap, with nobody watching. And then the crutch found the step again, and he got his good foot under him, and stood.
He stood there for a long time after that.
Thirty-one.
The steps turned.
At the forty-fourth step they came to a corner, where the old green wall on the left turned away, and the palace wall on the right went on, and the steps turned with it, to the right, round the corner of the palace. And at the corner there was a landing. A little square flat place, perhaps two paces across, where a man could stand and rest before he went on up. There was a stone seat built into the old wall, low and worn, with snow on it. Somebody had brushed the snow off one end of the seat. Not today. Some days ago. It had snowed again since, lightly, and the brushed place was only a little whiter than the rest.
And on the right, where the palace wall turned the corner, the wall was low.
Corin stood on the landing and looked at it.
All the way up the steps the palace wall had been three times the height of a man, smooth and blank and white. Here, at the corner, it came down. It came down to the height of his chest. And on top of it, set into the white stone, there was a row of iron railings. Black. Tall and thin and close together, each one ending in a little gilt spear point at the top, the same as the railings in front of every house on the Hill. Between the railings, through the gaps, there was light. Not the thin gray light of the stair. A wider light. An open light, with the whole gray sky in it.
He understood.
The steps had climbed all this way beside the east wing of the palace, the wing that stood out over the slope on its great stone arches. And here at the landing, at the forty-fourth step, they had climbed level with its roof.
He went to the railings. Crutch, good foot. He put his black hand on one of the cold iron bars. And he looked through.
He was looking at a garden.
It lay out in front of him on the flat roof of the east wing, long and narrow, perhaps forty paces long and fifteen across, with the low white wall and its railings going all the way round it, and beyond the wall on the far side, the sky, and the whole city spread out below it, falling away to the river, gray and white and smoking, as far as the Saltmarsh. Corin had never seen the city like that. From above. From the top. All of it at once.
But he did not look at the city. He looked at the garden.
It was a winter garden. Everything in it was asleep. And everything in it was very, very neat.
There were paths. Paths of pale gravel, raked so smooth that they looked like combed hair, with not a footprint on them, going round and between the beds in straight lines and careful curves. There were low hedges of box along the edges of the paths, dark green, clipped square, so square that they looked as if they had been cut out of green stone. There were beds. Long beds of bare black earth, edged with lines of white stones, each stone the same size as the next. Some of the beds had straw on them, laid down thick and even, tucked in at the edges like a blanket on a bed. Others had little mounds in them, in rows. Small mounds of earth, each one exactly the same size, in straight lines, a hand's width apart, all the way along the bed. Like a field of tiny graves.
There were rose bushes along the wall on the far side, cut back hard for the winter to a few thick black stumps each, and each stump wrapped in sacking and tied with string, the way you would wrap a hurt hand. There were three young trees in big stone pots, with their trunks wrapped too. In the middle of the garden there was a little round pool with a stone rim, frozen, with a stone fish in the middle of it standing on its tail, its mouth open to the sky. There was ice in its mouth.
At the far end of the garden, against the main wall of the palace, there was a glass house. A small one. Narrow and tall, with a curved glass roof, white-painted iron, and its glass misted on the inside so that Corin could only see shapes through it. Green shapes. Leaves. Something living in there, in the warm. In front of the glass house there was a pair of tall glass doors, closed, leading back into the palace. And a stone bench beside the doors, in the shelter of the wall, with a cushion on it. A gray cushion.
And beside the bench, on the gravel, there was a watering can.
It was very small. That was why he noticed it. It was a child's watering can, made of tin, painted white, the paint chipped. It had little flowers painted round it. Daisies. Yellow centers and white petals, done by hand, not very well, the way a child would paint them. It sat on the gravel by the bench as if somebody had only just put it down, and would be back for it in a moment.
Corin looked at it.
And inside him, very deep, behind everything, something went still.
Not quiet. He knew what it was like when Malakor was quiet. Malakor had been quiet for six days, ever since the wet door. Quiet was like an empty room. This was not an empty room. This was a room with someone in it who had stopped breathing. Who had heard a footstep on the stair, and gone rigid, and was standing behind the door in the dark with his hand over his own mouth.
Malakor? Corin thought.
Nothing.
Not nothing. Stillness. A held breath.
And from the far end of the garden, from somewhere near the glass house, where the paths went round the end of the long bed with the little mounds in it, Corin heard a sound.
The small sharp scrape of a trowel in frozen earth.
